steps.body: When two fractions share a denominator, their pieces are already the **same size** — you're just counting how many you have in all. 2/7 (two sevenths) plus 3/7 (three sevenths) is 5 sevenths: **5/7.** Add the numerators; the denominator — the piece size — never changes.
Add the pieces, keep the cut.

widget.prompt: 2/8 + 3/8. Build the answer on the bar.
widget.successFeedback: 5/8. The pieces are all the same size, so you just count them: 2 eighths plus 3 eighths is 5 eighths. The denominator names the piece — it is not something you add.
widget.lowFeedback: That is less than 5/8. Count the eighths: 2 + 3.
widget.highFeedback: That is more than 5/8. Adding the denominators too (5/16) is the classic slip — the bottom names the piece size, and that has not changed.

predict.prompt: The bar starts at 1/8. Before you touch it: is 1/8 more or less of the bar than 5/8?
predict.reveal: With the same whole, the bar settles it: 1/8 covers less than 5/8. Count of pieces and size of pieces work together — neither alone decides the amount. Here the pieces already match — both are eighths — so the count settles it: 5 pieces beat 1. It's when the pieces differ that the count alone can fool you.

steps.body: Here's why the denominator can't change: sevenths are sevenths. Combining 2 sevenths and 3 sevenths doesn't shrink the pieces into fourteenths — it just gives you more pieces of the SAME size. Adding the denominators (7+7=14) would mean the pieces got smaller, which never happened.

explanationVariants: Sam added the denominators too (7+7=14), but the pieces stayed the same size. The correct sum is 5/7.
Combining sevenths never turns them into fourteenths.

takeaways: Adding like fractions adds only the numerators.
The denominator names the piece size, which never changes.
Adding the denominators too is the classic trap — the pieces don't shrink when you combine them.
